Illustration by Daily Caller Staff; Source images from Eric Lee/Getty Images; DON EMMERT/AFP

Election Day is tomorrow. What happens after a blue wave? Poland may provide a preview.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin’s creepy and un-American screed in which she advocated for punishing young people for the crime of working for the Trump administration (“I want that deterrence message sent”) put Republicans on notice. Slotkin hinted she would like to seek prison sentences of up to 20 years for some Trump appointees.

The former (?) CIA officer has invoked Poland’s liberal Prime Minister Donald Tusk and his “iron broom” to “clean up” rightwing populism.

But just days before Americans go to the polls, Poland is undergoing a constitutional crisis.

Tusk — under the banner of “restoring the rule of law” — attempted to strengthen his grip over the country’s constitutional court.

Tusk’s 2023 election victory hinged on undoing the Law and Justice Party’s (PiS) changes, which emphasize patriotic sovereignty over European Union centralization. Promises made, promises kept: The PiS had resisted the EU’s changes to Poland’s high court. But a Tusk ally, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, tried to forcibly unseat its PiS-aligned chief justice while President Karol Nawrocki, allied with the PiS party, was out of the country.

The hostile takeover got physical when Nawrocki returned and tried to enter the court building and was shoved back by Korwin-Piotrowska and a police cordon. He eventually got inside anyway. He held crisis talks at the presidential palace, but members of Tusk’s coalition reportedly didn’t show up.

Tusk has used the term “demokracja walcząca,” militant democracy, implying the ends of “saving democracy” justify any undemocratic means.

The parallels between the efforts to defang PiS in Warsaw and “Trump-proof” Washington are too obvious to miss: Tusk co-wrote a book with Trump critic, “authoritarianism expert” and globalist par excellence Anne Applebaum.

If Democrats win control of Congress and wield committee gavels, will they simply be fulfilling their checks-and-balances duty to oversee the Executive Branch?

Or is Slotkin’s invocation of Tusk’s “iron broom” a sign that some Democrats are engaged in the same winner-takes-all, take-no-prisoners battle to criminalize the MAGA movement and right-wing populism? And does it lead to the same chaos?

As Poland faces a constitutional crisis, French riots roll into their third week, and Brazilian opposition leaders leave the country, the Free World has become a tinderbox — and the left has shown that they’re eager to light it.

President Donald Trump held rallies in Kansas and Iowa yesterday.

Trump will give his closing message ahead of Tuesday’s election at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Iran War May Reach Fever Pitch After The Midterms

With the Iran War reportedly costing the average American household $2,000, it’s been a big thorn in Republicans’ side this election cycle. However, there are some signs that it’s not going to get yanked out anytime soon.

The bullet point list makers at Axios reported Sunday that President Trump had a “candid” phone call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday in which Netanyahu urged Trump to strike Iran immediately after the midterm elections. That would be Nov. 4, just six days before the new Knesset is expected to be sworn in. Netanyahu’s hold on power remains uncertain after he did not secure enough votes to put together a winning coalition in Israel’s parliamentary election last week. Should his chief opponent Gadi Eisenkot put together a coalition, it would usher in an official inquiry into why the Netanyahu government did not anticipate the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks.

“We may do another little Epic Fury,” Trump said earlier this month. He may target Pickaxe Mountain, but there is uncertainty over whether even powerful American bunker busters could sufficiently penetrate it.

In return, Iran has promised attacks on US ships, on underwater internet cables, and on critical energy facilities of Gulf allies.

Democratic Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy — who was hospitalized yesterday after having a stroke — made waves after a Wednesday panel at the Middle East Institute (MEI). He said that in a classified setting he learned about the plan should the Trump administration reengage in kinetic war. He described it as “insane.” He said it would lead to the “destruction of our commitment to the rule of law” in that the military would attack civilian targets.

Murphy said that he was barred from observing the damage at the U.S. base in Qatar or from speaking to Pentagon officials there. Murphy sits on the subcommittee that oversees defense spending.

Critics like former counterintelligence official Joe Kent have proposed that Trump simply declare victory and extricate himself.

Meanwhile Vice President Vance sent a letter to Iran’s national security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, asking about restarting negotiations.

Yet Trump seems to be indicating a willingness to target civilians, just as Murphy indicated: “I could have won the Vietnam War in a week … Agent Orange, they drop it in the forests for years and years and years instead of going after Ho Chi Minh City.”

Both chambers of Congress are scheduled to return from recess on Nov. 9. Until then, Republicans are fighting to defend their majorities on the campaign trail. Democrats only need to net three seats in the House and four seats in the Senate to wrest control of Capitol Hill.

The Cook Political Report’s Friday forecast paints a bleak picture for Republicans. Democrats appear ahead in 16 Republican-held House seats. Meanwhile, six Republican-held Senate seats appear to be “toss-ups” and one is rated as a “likely” Democrat gain.

Speaker Mike Johnson, however, told Fox News last Monday that polls have been “even further off this time because more and more Republicans are unwilling to participate in these surveys.”

“They don’t want to give their information to someone on the phone,” Johnson continued. “They’re calling it the partisan nonresponse bias.”

A blue wave would usher in a subpoena tsunami in the Congress and Democrats can’t help but spill some of their priorities.

Slotkin has named a handful of “signature cases” that a Democrat-controlled Senate could prosecute: former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s taxpayer-supported television ads, Department of the Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s contract for the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, and U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s promise to investigate Slotkin for advocating for insurrection.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal has promised an expansion of his investigation into the White House ballroom.

And Rep. Ro Khanna wants a rather broad Truth and Accountability Commission to investigate not just the Iran War but also DOGE’s government cost cutting and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) deportations, invoking the language of “transitional justice” usually reserved for history’s bloodiest atrocities like Pinochet’s dictatorship in Chile. Does asking government employees to describe what they do all day constitute a crime against humanity?

Then again, why stop there? The American Constitution Society, a Big Law-supported counterpart to the Federalist Society, wants Democrats to go bigger, proposing a Truth and Reconciliation Commission for people to air grievances about “the history of America” that would usher in sweeping changes to our institutions.

Michigan Democrats Divided Over Everybody’s Favorite Topic

Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed during the August primary, endorsed Republican nominee Mike Rogers yesterday.

“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” Stevens said. “I do not stand with Hasan Piker who gets trafficked on our college campuses. A dear friend of mine earlier today was saying that education is on the ballot — and she’s absolutely right. And what our students see, what our children see, and who we are as Michiganders is not hate. And is not what we’re getting out from our Democratic nominee right now.”

I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today. https://t.co/pQgfSBuhOJ

This came in response to El-Sayed’s campaign telling Stevens to stay away from its events following a feud between the two over an ad by Rebellion PAC, where a woman claimed she couldn’t afford eggs because she had to set aside tax money for “killing Palestinians.”

Rebellion PAC is owned by “The Young Turks” co-founder Cenk Uygur, the uncle of far-left streamer Hasan Piker.

Rock n roll. Life is good.

While El-Sayed’s campaign disavowed the ad, the Democratic nominee fired back against Stevens on X last Friday.

“Our campaign is and has always been focused on addressing the most critical challenges Michiganders are facing: Skyrocketing gas prices, unaffordable groceries, and the inability to see a doctor,” El-Sayed wrote. “That focus is why our people-powered campaign defeated a historic $70M in outside spending from big corporations and AIPAC [the American Israel Public Affairs Committee] on behalf of Congresswoman Stevens.”

A Rogers campaign spokesperson, Abigail Ronson — who is allegedly a registered agent for Israel — shared an image on X of Stevens alongside the Republican nominee in a Detroit church pew Sunday morning.

HAPPENING NOW: Congresswoman Haley Stevens joins Mike Rogers at church in Detroit this morning. We have a state to save, Michigan. https://t.co/ZE2HJ1XfHP

“Something snapped in her,” said former Gov. Jim Blanchard, who had dinner with Stevens and her fiance on Friday. He said that the fiance, Jason Turkish, was critical of her decision to endorse El-Sayed.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who arguably stands to benefit the most from flipping the upper chamber, called Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers “a despicable betrayal” on X hours later.

“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors,” the New York Democrat wrote.

Last Monday, we highlighted the lawsuit that the Department of Justice plans to trigger against Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses because of a candidate who shares his name. Obama-appointed U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason threw it out yesterday. However, that wasn’t the only blow Republicans received from the judiciary ahead of Election Day.

Last-Minute Ruling Slows Trump Admin’s Ad Blitz

New York-based U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon ruled for three of the Trump admin’s campaign ads to be pulled from the airwaves, The Associated Press (AP) reported Friday.

These included ads titled “$5,000 to Americans,” “Every Democrat Voted Against No Tax on Tips,” and “Cost of Socialism.”

The temporary restraining order came after the watchdog group Common Cause filed a lawsuit aiming to pull thirteen ads that they alleged were on government websites, according to AP.

“This Biden-appointed activist judge issued a lawless order to stop the administration from sharing patriotic videos,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told AP.

This ruling could deal a blow to the GOP’s already disadvantaged ad blitz. Over 70% of respondents POLITICO polled from Oct. 3-5 reported seeing more ads for Democrats than Republicans this election cycle.

State-Level Supreme Court Strikes GOP Mail-In Ballot Lawsuit

The GOP was dealt another blow in the judiciary last Thursday when the Michigan Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal of a ruling that struck the Republican National Committee’s lawsuit against Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson’s guidance on how to read mismatched mail-in ballots, Michigan Advance reported.

The order’s lack of a majority opinion prompted backlash from Justice Brian Zahra — the court’s lone Republican.

“As Michigan’s court of last resort we owe it to the people of Michigan to explain why ballots with mismatched or missing ballot numbers are tabulated when our Legislature has plainly stated that ‘[i]f the ballot numbers match, the board of election inspectors shall … prepare the ballot for tabulation,’” Zahra wrote.

Michigan is among the 24 states with state-level supreme court elections this year, according to Ballotpedia, with six candidates competing for two out of the court’s seven seats.

The Not-So-Democratic Party

If Democrats seize control of Congress this Tuesday, government officials may not be the only ones facing their wrath, but private citizens too. One likely target is Elon Musk, who The New York Times reported spent over $276 million on the midterm elections.

Conservative-leaning comedian Tim Dillon predicted on his show last Saturday that Musk may flee the United States after his work as DOGE’s mastermind coupled with his substantial campaign contributions to Republicans painted a target on his back.

“He might leave the country. You might start seeing that now,” Dillon said. “And this is when you know things are getting really interesting is, like, some of these guys that go really hard for one party and then fund that party, get that party elected, and then run around the government playing president for a few months — which is what that guy did — they might just have to skedaddle when the next party comes in.”

Multiple Democrats in Congress are already gearing up to investigate Musk over his five-month foray at DOGE, POLITICO reported Oct. 20. These include (but aren’t limited to) Democratic Reps. Zoe Lofgren and Greg Meeks, who are ranking members on their respective committees.

We saw a similar situation in Brazil, when Brazilian Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro fled to Miami after losing to left-wing Brazilian President Lula da Silva on Oct. 25. Both Lula and Bolsonaro’s father, former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, were previously arrested by Brazil’s government.

Citing Brazil as an example, Dillon warned that this is “how states fail.”

“So, once the two parties start imprisoning each other — and they’re not really parties as we understand them, they’re just factions or power factions — and one has the upper hand and starts imprisoning the other one, it goes back and forth until one party holds power and maintains it and says, ‘F*** it. I’m not leaving because if I leave, I’m going to jail,’” Dillon continued. “And that’s how you slide into like a fascistic situation or a communist situation [sic].”

Musk himself expressed a similar concern on X last Friday, warning that if Democrats make a “clean sweep” of Congress and the Presidency, they’ll expand their majority by granting DC and Puerto Rico statehood, open our borders to mass migration, and pack the Supreme Court.

My biggest concern is that if there is a clean sweep by Democrats of the House, Senate and Presidency in 2028, they will: 1. Make DC and Puerto Rico states to gain a strong majority in the Senate. 2. Open the borders and legalize everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority. 3. Increase the size of the Supreme Court to gain an immediate majority. This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word. All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029. That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election. Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one.

“This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word,” Musk wrote.

My biggest concern is that if there is a clean sweep by Democrats of the House, Senate and Presidency in 2028, they will: 1. Make DC and Puerto Rico states to gain a strong majority in the Senate. 2. Open the borders and legalize everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority. 3. Increase the size of the Supreme Court to gain an immediate majority. This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word. All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029. That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election. Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one.

“This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word,” Musk wrote.

news.originalContent:
President Donald Trump’s low approval ratings, mirroring Americans’ sentiments about the economy, are looming over the 2026 midterms and Republicans’ chances of maintaining control of Congress.

NBC News’s chief data analyst, Steve Kornacki, presented the outlet’s final poll during Sunday’s episode of “Meet The Press.” He noted Trump’s approval ratings have declined going into his second term’s midterm elections, echoing respondents’ dissatisfaction with their personal finances and the economy for the first time in 30 years.

Historically, Trump’s biggest selling point to voters has been his handling of the economy. Ahead of the midterms, however, nearly three quarters of respondents (73%) indicated they were dissatisfied by the effects of the affordability crisis.

“[C]ompare this to Trump’s first midterm in 2018,” Kornacki observed while pointing to a series of poll results displayed on a large screen. “I think this is why his standing in that approval rating is lower now. Because, look at this, in 2018 the economy was his strong suit: nearly 70% of voters on the eve of that midterm were satisfied with it. Total opposite right now. And then there is this one: your own personal financial situation: 49[%] satisfied, 51[%] dissatisfied. This 51% figure that you see right here for ‘dissatisfied,’ that is the first time in over 30 years of the NBC poll that the dissatisfaction number has been at that level, has been a majority.”

Overall, President Trump’s pre-election approval rating sits at 40 percent approval. Despite this low rating, when asked which party would do a better job on key issues, poll respondents still found that the Republican Party would be more favorable in terms of handling the economy, government corruption, and immigration. Respondents also said, however, the Democratic Party would be preferable in addressing the war with Iran and inflation, signaling a shift in satisfaction trends.

“But which party would do a better job on key issues?” Kornacki previewed. “This also tells the story here. When it comes to inflation, Democrats [have] an advantage of a point. That may not seem like much, but this was, like, a 20-point advantage for Republicans just a couple years ago as Trump was returning to the White House. Same thing here on the economy: that is a two-point advantage for [Democrats]. But again, this was Trump’s strong suit, this has historically been a strong suit. For those to even be close, that represents ground gained by Democrats.”

“Is there hope for Republicans?” he comcluded. “The one number they would point to would simply be, and this is a difference from 2018, the image of the two political parties here. Republicans are not popular, but their number, overall as a party, their favorable, unfavorable number [is] about where it was in 2018. The Democrats, though, Kristen, [are] only 29% favorable right now. That’s different than 2018, and that is one of the questions heading into Tuesday. In ‘18, the Democrats, as a party they were positioned to take votes from voters who were dissatisfied with Trump. Does the Democratic Party have more baggage now in a way that will prevent it from capitalizing on all of these other numbers we’re showing you?”

news.originalContent:
Several key races on Tuesday will determine if Republicans were able to beat expectations after trailing Democrats in the polls.

The elections appeared grim for Republicans in both the House and Senate races, particularly as voters remained dissatisfied with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy. The races in deep-red states and districts, such as Ohio, Kansas and Texas, as well as in battleground states like Michigan, will be the most anticipated matchups to watch Tuesday night.

The Alaska Senate race has been embroiled in legal woes and investigations after The New York Times reported that former Democratic Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola’s campaign and aides with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) coordinated to recruit other Republican candidates to run against Republican Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan. Former schoolteacher Dan J. Sullivan entered the race in June and will appear on the ballot, which could confuse voters into voting for the wrong Sullivan.

Aides with the DSCC introduced Democratic operative Jerid Kurtz to former members of Peltola’s team, who informed them he was in contact with another Sullivan from Petersburg. He attempted to recruit other Alaskans to run as Republicans by traveling to several communities and meeting different individuals in casual settings. (RELATED: Secret Scheme To Sabotage GOP Senator Revealed After Democrat Denied Involvement: REPORT)

Matthew Salisbury of Anchorage told the Times that he got a call from an unfamiliar number with an Ohio area code. The person, who identified himself as Zane, met with him at a pub and urged him to run for Senate. When the Times showed Salisbury a photograph of Kurtz, Salisbury confirmed that Kurtz was the person in question.

Alaska’s open voting system made this scheme possible, given that candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves, according to the Times. Republicans backed an effort to help a candite serving time in a New York prison stay on the ballot when Peltola ran for reelection to the House in 2024.

The Department of Justice subpoenaed over three dozen individuals as part of its investigation into the Democrats’ scheme. Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the scheme violated any laws.

Today’s New York Times reporting reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates—including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator—to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes. The Alaska Division of Elections investigated these very concerns in June of this year. The new reporting substantially supports the Division’s findings. I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted. The evidence will determine what happens next. Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support. Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections. Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.

Peltola led by an average of 1.2 points as of Friday, though it remains to be seen how the Times’ report will impact her chances.

The other Sullivan’s candidacy prompted legal action to be taken over the summer. Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher informed Sullivan in an Aug. 26 letter that his declaration of candidacy “was not filed in order to declare an actual good-faith candidacy,” but rather to confuse voters into voting for the wrong Sullivan. After Sullivan appealed the ruling, Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews ruled he could remain on the ballot for the state’s primary.

The Alaska Supreme Court overturned that ruling in a June 30 decision and allowed the other Sullivan to be on the ballot. The DSCC and Peltola’s campaign celebrated the high court’s decision, according to the Times.

The other Sullivan changed his party affiliation from Republican to unaffiliated on Wednesday.

Democratic strategist Amber Lee authored a press release announcing the other Sullivan’s candidacy, metadata reviewed by the DCNF showed. Lee told The Hill in January that she believed there was a good chance Peltola could defeat Sullivan and previously hoped Peltola would run for governor.

Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed and former Republican Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers face a tight competition to replace Democratic Michigan Sen. Gary Peters. El-Sayed, a political newcomer who ran as the anti-establishment candidate, defeated Democratic Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens by one point in the Democratic primary after receiving endorsements from independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Democratic Michigan Rep. Rashida Tlaib.

The race will determine whether an anti-establishment Democrat can defeat an establishment, traditional Republican in a battleground state that President Donald Trump won by one point in 2024. El-Sayed would have to win over enough non-college educated, non-white and lower income voters to win, although he struggled with these voters during August’s Democratic primary.

Stevens won more than 50% of the vote in counties where less than 30% had a college education, while El-Sayed won nearly 60% of the vote in counties where at least 30% of residents held a bachelor’s degree, according to Politico. He also won in areas with universities while further-left candidates performed well with young voters and underperformed with black voters.

The Michigan Democrat held a 3.2-point lead against Rogers as of Friday, according to RealClearPolling. El-Sayed centered his campaign around affordability, fighting corporate money in politics and opposing the political establishment. He also supported cutting off aid to Israel and condemned the Iran war.

Rogers received an endorsement from Trump, although he broke with Trump during the general election cycle on the Iran war and Canadian tariffs. Rogers’ campaign released an advertisement on Oct. 8 that called for an end to a “tariff war” with Canada to help lower prices for consumers in the state, given that the state’s economy is strongly tied to the neighboring country.

Trump announced in July that 50% tariffs would be imposed on various Canadian goods, including wood and large motorcycles, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, to force trade concessions. He implemented bans on specific Canadian alcohol, dairy and motorcycle products that went into effect on Sept. 29.

Rogers backed the tariffs in an Aug. 29 statement, stating they were “necessary” for Michigan’s economy.

“President Trump is right to put America First - and tariffs are necessary, but are not a size-fits-all solution,” Rogers said. “Elissa Slotkin and Gary Peters are missing in action. Michigan deserves a Senator who will work with President Trump to broker a trade deal with Canada that supports our farmers and gets the best deal for Michigan autoworkers and manufacturers.”

Rogers flip-flopped on the Iran war, stating in a Sept. 21 ad that it needed to end to bring costs down. He previously described Iran as an “imminent threat” and called U.S. military action a “win-win-win” for the nation.

Democratic voters largely voted out establishment incumbents and replaced them with further-left candidates, such as El-Sayed. Many in the Democratic coalition have increasingly become opposed to aiding Israel, which appeared evident when over 100 Democratic representatives voted for Republican Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie’s amendment that would have slashed $3.3 billion in foreign aid to Israel.

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent $30.6 million during the primary season, spending over $20 million opposing El-Sayed and over $10 million supporting Stevens, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings. Rogers’ allies told AIPAC in August not to advertise on his behalf after El-Sayed won, although he said during an Oct. 9 debate that he welcomed support from AIPAC and anyone else who wanted to help his campaign.

AIPAC reportedly planned to give up to $9 million to a pro-Rogers super PAC, the Great Lakes Conservative Fund, in late October, anonymous sources told The New York Times. The spending was deliberately timed for after the Oct. 14 deadline so it would not appear on FEC filings before Election Day.

Current FEC filings do not show any contribution from AIPAC or UDP going to Rogers’ super PAC. UDP spent $95,000 on mailers to oppose El-Sayed on Oct. 9.

The race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic Texas state Rep. James Talarico remains tight, despite Texas being a traditionally red state.

Republicans spent over $300 million to help Paxton defeat Talarico. Texas has not had a Democratic senator since 1993, and Republicans control the state Legislature, attorney general’s and governor’s offices.

Talarico led Paxton by an average of 1.8 points as of Friday, according to RealClearPolling. The tight race has made Democrats hopeful they could flip a Senate seat blue for the first time in over three decades, prompting them to spend over $130 million in ad spending.

Corruption became a top issue for voters in the final stretch before the election, which likely hurt Paxton’s candidacy. The Republican-controlled Texas state Legislature impeached Paxton in 2023 on bribery and abuse of power charges, although the state Senate acquitted him.

Paxton was accused of misusing the office of the attorney general to protect and assist Austin real estate developer and political donor Nate Paul, who faced federal investigations. He allegedly intervened in lawsuits, issued favorable legal opinions to protect Paul’s properties from foreclosure and hired a special prosecutor to investigate claims helpful to Paul.

Paul allegedly paid for expensive renovations to Paxton’s home and employed a woman with whom Paxton had an extramarital affair. Paxton denied all wrongdoing.

Talarico repeatedly accused Paxton of being a corrupt politician who has used his power to get richer. Paxton’s net worth rose from $174,000 when he first entered the state Legislature in 2003 to an estimated $13 million currently, according to Forbes.

An October University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll found voters trusted Talarico more on handling corruption than Paxton by ten percentage points.

Talarico stated in 2021 that God was “non-binary” and that transgender children were made in His image. He claimed that the biblical account of Jesus’ conception justified abortion and also said on a May 2023 podcast that he loved transgender kids when asked to name something he loved other than his family and friends.

Paxton argued on the campaign trail that Talarico is too liberal for Texas.

The Texas Democrat left the campaign trail for nine days during the first week of October, claiming he had a “nasty case of the flu.”

Paxton defeated Republican Texas Sen. John Cornyn by a 28-point margin in May after Trump endorsed him last-minute. During the Republican primary, Republican Texas Sen. John Cornyn and his allies referred to Paxton as “Crooked Ken” and called him “corrupt to the core” in one ad. Talarico and his allies released attack ads calling out Paxton’s alleged corruption.

Ohio Senate & Governor’s races

Democrats are eyeing Ohio as a potential win against Republicans, who control the state Legislature and governor’s office. Former Democratic Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown and Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton held slight leads in the polls against Republican Ohio Sen. Jon Husted and Republican Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.

Brown led Husted by an average of 2.6 points, according to RealClearPolling. Trump won Ohio by a twelve-point margin, 55.2% to 43.9%. Husted assumed office in January 2025 to replace Vice President J.D. Vance.

Acton led Ramaswamy by an average of 4.3 points as of Friday, according to RealClearPolling. Ramaswamy faced backlash after an advertisement featuring Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, telling voters not to vote for her.

Acton and her mother have been estranged since 1978, when she was 12 years old. She and her younger brother were removed from Arthur’s custody after her husband was charged with sexually abusing Acton.

Ramaswamy’s poll numbers dropped six points Thursday after the ad aired, according to Truthout.

Republican Maine Sen. Susan Collins faces a tough challenge against Democratic Maine Senate candidate Troy Jackson, who entered the race late in the game. Heating fuel prices became a top issue for Maine voters since the Iran war began, which could give Democrats an advantage in the deep blue state.

Jackson held a slight lead over Collins in the deep-blue state, holding a 1.4 point average lead, according to RealClearPolling. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won Maine by a 52.4% to 45.5% margin in the 2024 election. Maine Democrats control the governor’s office, attorney general’s office and the state Legislature.

Despite Maine being a blue state, Collins has won five Senate races since 1996.

The two candidates both campaigned on the high cost of living, particularly the high-heating costs in Maine. The average statewide heating fuel prices rose to $6.05 per gallon as of Oct. 26. Roughly half of the population in Maine rely on heating oil as their principal energy source in the winter, meaning they could face an increase of thousands of dollars in heating.

The Iran war caused heating fuel prices to soar, given that the Strait of Hormuz handles roughly 20% to 25% of the world’s seaborne oil and petroleum product flow. Collins voted to extend U.S. military operations in Iran five times since February.

Collins and independent Maine Sen. Angus King urged the Trump administration to tap into the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to help lower costs before the elections. She joined a bipartisan push to expedite the release of over $38 million in federal home heating assistance for Maine households.

Collins initially ran against former Democratic Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race after a woman accused him of rape.

Republican Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall is trailing Democratic Kansas Senate nominee Adam Hamilton by an average of 2.6 points. A Democratic victory would be a major upset, given that Kansas has not had a Democratic senator since 1939.

The Republican senator sued 700 of his patients for outstanding debts during his time as an OB-GYN, which led to 81 arrests, The New York Times reported. Some facing lawsuits were mothers with outstanding bills from their deliveries, and many patients lacked insurance. One mother had a nine-month-old baby when her bank account was garnished.

Marshall paid a bakery $1,300 after its owner, Holly Thomas, accused his 2020 campaign of leaving a nearly $700 bill unpaid for six years. The senator said on X that he paid the bill and apologized to the bakery, claiming he had “no idea” how the bill went unpaid for six years.

RealClearPolling averages showed Marshall and Hamilton in a tie in mid-October.

The close race caused the Senate Leadership Fund, Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, to spend $14 million to support Marshall.

The Senate Majority PAC, the Democrats’ Senate campaign arm, launched a $5 million statewide television advertising campaign that plans to run through Election Day, indicating that Democrats were increasingly confident they could flip the seat, Politico reported. One ad attacked Marshall for voting against an amendment that would require the Department of Justice (DOJ) to release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The PAC’s research found that Epstein ads can sway elections three to six points in the Democrats’ direction.

The economy remained a top issue for Kansas voters, according to an Emerson College poll from Thursday. Diesel prices averaged $6.03 per gallon in Kansas, which Marshall largely attributed to the war in Ukraine. Hamilton pinned the high Diesel prices on Trump and the Iran war, which has likely resonated with farmers across the state.

Elections forecasters projected that Democrats would retake the House in the next Congress. Republicans redrew several districts to give themselves an advantage in November, but many Republican-held seats are still at risk of flipping for Democrats.

Republicans hoped to flip Democratic Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz’s seat in Florida’s 25th district. The state redrew the district with hopes that a Republican could pick up the seat, although Cook Political Report moved the race from the “Toss Up” column to “Lean Democratic.”

The Congressional Leadership Fund, the top House super PAC, slashed $6 million in ad spending in the district to oppose Moskowitz, who is running against former Republican Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer. The No Going Back PAC, a super PAC backed by MAGA Inc., planned to spend $6.3 million in the district.

The super PAC also slashed $3 million from Texas’ 28th district, which was redrawn to help Republicans oust Democratic Texas Rep. Henry Cuellar. Trump won the district by seven percentage points in 2024.

Cook Political Report shifted the races in Arizona’s sixth district, Colorado’s eighth district, Virginia’s second district and Wisconsin’s third district into the “Lean Democratic” column less than two weeks before Election Day. Republican Reps. Juan Ciscomani of Arizona, Gabe Evans of Colorado, Jen Kiggans of Virginia and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin currently hold those seats.

Eight Republican-held seats shifted in Democrats’ favor, including Republican Pennsylvania Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick’s seat in Pennsylvania’s first district and Republican Indiana Rep. Victoria Spartz’s seat in Indiana’s fifth district, according to Cook Political Report. The projection would give Democrats up to 240 seats in the House in the next Congress if they flip between 12 and 25 seats.

Republican Ohio Rep. Max Miller could lose to Democratic Ohio congressional nominee Brian Poindexter in Ohio’s 7th district, where Trump won by 10.6 percentage points in 2024. Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, accused him of domestic abuse, which Miller repeatedly denied.

Miller refused to drop out of the race when some in his party called on him to drop out. Among those who called on him to drop out included Husted and Miller’s ex-father-in-law, Republican Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno. Miller did not exit the race by the necessary deadline for Ohio’s Republican party to replace him, meaning Poindexter would have remained uncontested if Miller had exited the race.

Poindexter out-raised Miller by a wide margin in the third quarter. The Democrat reported $2.47 million in receipts and $1.72 million in spending between July 1 and September 30, while Miller raised $1.14 million and ended September with about $944,000 on hand.

Republican New York Rep. Mike Lawler faces a competitive reelection bid against Democratic New York congressional nominee Cait Conley in New York’s 17th district. He is one of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents since Harris won his district in the 2024 election by less than one point, although former President Joe Biden won it by ten points in 2020.

The candidates were neck-and-neck as of Friday. A McLaughlin & Associates survey from late September showed Lawler leading by three points, while an Emerson College poll showed Conley leading by two points.

Lawler painted Conley as a radical socialist on the campaign trail, while Conley tied Lawler to Trump. The district is one of the most centrist in the U.S.

Democratic New York Rep. Tom Suozzi is defending his seat in New York’s third district against former Republican New York state Assemblyman Michael LiPetri. Suozzi, who replaced former Republican New York Rep. George Santos after he was expelled from Congress, narrowly won his seat in 2024 by a three-point margin. The No Going Back PAC, a super PAC tied to Trump’s political organization MAGA Inc., spent nearly $8 million to support LiPetri, which included $5.7 million in ad spending to attack Suozzi.

Republican New York congressional nominee Anthony Constantino and Democratic New York congressional nominee Blake Gendebien are running for an open seat in New York’s 21st district after Republican New York Rep. Elise Stefanik decided not to run. While traditionally a Republican district, the candidates are neck-and-neck while tariffs, the economy and relations with Canada remained top issues.

A Public Policy Polling survey from mid-October found Constantino leading by two points, while a New York Times/Siena College poll showed Gendebien leading by four points.

Republican Pennsylvania Rep. Rob Bresnahan is defending his seat against Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti in Pennsylvania’s 8th district. The cost of living remained the top issue in the district, prompting Bresnahan to call on the Iran war to come to an immediate end. About two-thirds of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, which is expected to cost many Republicans House seats.

An Emerson College poll showed Cognetti leading 52% to 48%, while A New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University poll found her ahead by a 51% to 46% margin.

Republican Michigan Rep. Tom Barrett is facing off with Democratic Michigan congressional nominee William Lawrence, a further-left political activist, in Michigan’s seventh district. Lawrence co-founded the Sunrise Movement, an organization that advocates for action on climate change.

Recent polls showed Lawrence leading Barrett, including an Emerson College poll where Lawrence led by eight points.

Democratic strategist Amber Lee authored a press release announcing the other Sullivan’s candidacy, metadata reviewed by the DCNF showed. Lee told The Hill in January that she believed there was a good chance Peltola could defeat Sullivan and previously hoped Peltola would run for governor.

Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed and former Republican Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers face a tight competition to replace Democratic Michigan Sen. Gary Peters. El-Sayed, a political newcomer who ran as the anti-establishment candidate, defeated Democratic Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens by one point in the Democratic primary after receiving endorsements from independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Democratic Michigan Rep. Rashida Tlaib.

The race will determine whether an anti-establishment Democrat can defeat an establishment, traditional Republican in a battleground state that President Donald Trump won by one point in 2024. El-Sayed would have to win over enough non-college educated, non-white and lower income voters to win, although he struggled with these voters during August’s Democratic primary.

Stevens won more than 50% of the vote in counties where less than 30% had a college education, while El-Sayed won nearly 60% of the vote in counties where at least 30% of residents held a bachelor’s degree, according to Politico. He also won in areas with universities while further-left candidates performed well with young voters and underperformed with black voters.

The Michigan Democrat held a 3.2-point lead against Rogers as of Friday, according to RealClearPolling. El-Sayed centered his campaign around affordability, fighting corporate money in politics and opposing the political establishment. He also supported cutting off aid to Israel and condemned the Iran war.

Rogers received an endorsement from Trump, although he broke with Trump during the general election cycle on the Iran war and Canadian tariffs. Rogers’ campaign released an advertisement on Oct. 8 that called for an end to a “tariff war” with Canada to help lower prices for consumers in the state, given that the state’s economy is strongly tied to the neighboring country.

Trump announced in July that 50% tariffs would be imposed on various Canadian goods, including wood and large motorcycles, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, to force trade concessions. He implemented bans on specific Canadian alcohol, dairy and motorcycle products that went into effect on Sept. 29.

Rogers backed the tariffs in an Aug. 29 statement, stating they were “necessary” for Michigan’s economy.

“President Trump is right to put America First - and tariffs are necessary, but are not a size-fits-all solution,” Rogers said. “Elissa Slotkin and Gary Peters are missing in action. Michigan deserves a Senator who will work with President Trump to broker a trade deal with Canada that supports our farmers and gets the best deal for Michigan autoworkers and manufacturers.”

Rogers flip-flopped on the Iran war, stating in a Sept. 21 ad that it needed to end to bring costs down. He previously described Iran as an “imminent threat” and called U.S. military action a “win-win-win” for the nation.

Democratic voters largely voted out establishment incumbents and replaced them with further-left candidates, such as El-Sayed. Many in the Democratic coalition have increasingly become opposed to aiding Israel, which appeared evident when over 100 Democratic representatives voted for Republican Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie’s amendment that would have slashed $3.3 billion in foreign aid to Israel.

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent $30.6 million during the primary season, spending over $20 million opposing El-Sayed and over $10 million supporting Stevens, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings. Rogers’ allies told AIPAC in August not to advertise on his behalf after El-Sayed won, although he said during an Oct. 9 debate that he welcomed support from AIPAC and anyone else who wanted to help his campaign.

AIPAC reportedly planned to give up to $9 million to a pro-Rogers super PAC, the Great Lakes Conservative Fund, in late October, anonymous sources told The New York Times. The spending was deliberately timed for after the Oct. 14 deadline so it would not appear on FEC filings before Election Day.

Current FEC filings do not show any contribution from AIPAC or UDP going to Rogers’ super PAC. UDP spent $95,000 on mailers to oppose El-Sayed on Oct. 9.

The race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic Texas state Rep. James Talarico remains tight, despite Texas being a traditionally red state.

Republicans spent over $300 million to help Paxton defeat Talarico. Texas has not had a Democratic senator since 1993, and Republicans control the state Legislature, attorney general’s and governor’s offices.

Talarico led Paxton by an average of 1.8 points as of Friday, according to RealClearPolling. The tight race has made Democrats hopeful they could flip a Senate seat blue for the first time in over three decades, prompting them to spend over $130 million in ad spending.

Corruption became a top issue for voters in the final stretch before the election, which likely hurt Paxton’s candidacy. The Republican-controlled Texas state Legislature impeached Paxton in 2023 on bribery and abuse of power charges, although the state Senate acquitted him.

Paxton was accused of misusing the office of the attorney general to protect and assist Austin real estate developer and political donor Nate Paul, who faced federal investigations. He allegedly intervened in lawsuits, issued favorable legal opinions to protect Paul’s properties from foreclosure and hired a special prosecutor to investigate claims helpful to Paul.

Paul allegedly paid for expensive renovations to Paxton’s home and employed a woman with whom Paxton had an extramarital affair. Paxton denied all wrongdoing.

Talarico repeatedly accused Paxton of being a corrupt politician who has used his power to get richer. Paxton’s net worth rose from $174,000 when he first entered the state Legislature in 2003 to an estimated $13 million currently, according to Forbes.

An October University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll found voters trusted Talarico more on handling corruption than Paxton by ten percentage points.

Talarico stated in 2021 that God was “non-binary” and that transgender children were made in His image. He claimed that the biblical account of Jesus’ conception justified abortion and also said on a May 2023 podcast that he loved transgender kids when asked to name something he loved other than his family and friends.

Paxton argued on the campaign trail that Talarico is too liberal for Texas.

The Texas Democrat left the campaign trail for nine days during the first week of October, claiming he had a “nasty case of the flu.”

Paxton defeated Republican Texas Sen. John Cornyn by a 28-point margin in May after Trump endorsed him last-minute. During the Republican primary, Republican Texas Sen. John Cornyn and his allies referred to Paxton as “Crooked Ken” and called him “corrupt to the core” in one ad. Talarico and his allies released attack ads calling out Paxton’s alleged corruption.

Ohio Senate & Governor’s races

Democrats are eyeing Ohio as a potential win against Republicans, who control the state Legislature and governor’s office. Former Democratic Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown and Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton held slight leads in the polls against Republican Ohio Sen. Jon Husted and Republican Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.

Brown led Husted by an average of 2.6 points, according to RealClearPolling. Trump won Ohio by a twelve-point margin, 55.2% to 43.9%. Husted assumed office in January 2025 to replace Vice President J.D. Vance.

Acton led Ramaswamy by an average of 4.3 points as of Friday, according to RealClearPolling. Ramaswamy faced backlash after an advertisement featuring Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, telling voters not to vote for her.

Acton and her mother have been estranged since 1978, when she was 12 years old. She and her younger brother were removed from Arthur’s custody after her husband was charged with sexually abusing Acton.

Ramaswamy’s poll numbers dropped six points Thursday after the ad aired, according to Truthout.

Republican Maine Sen. Susan Collins faces a tough challenge against Democratic Maine Senate candidate Troy Jackson, who entered the race late in the game. Heating fuel prices became a top issue for Maine voters since the Iran war began, which could give Democrats an advantage in the deep blue state.

Jackson held a slight lead over Collins in the deep-blue state, holding a 1.4 point average lead, according to RealClearPolling. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won Maine by a 52.4% to 45.5% margin in the 2024 election. Maine Democrats control the governor’s office, attorney general’s office and the state Legislature.

Despite Maine being a blue state, Collins has won five Senate races since 1996.

The two candidates both campaigned on the high cost of living, particularly the high-heating costs in Maine. The average statewide heating fuel prices rose to $6.05 per gallon as of Oct. 26. Roughly half of the population in Maine rely on heating oil as their principal energy source in the winter, meaning they could face an increase of thousands of dollars in heating.

The Iran war caused heating fuel prices to soar, given that the Strait of Hormuz handles roughly 20% to 25% of the world’s seaborne oil and petroleum product flow. Collins voted to extend U.S. military operations in Iran five times since February.

Collins and independent Maine Sen. Angus King urged the Trump administration to tap into the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to help lower costs before the elections. She joined a bipartisan push to expedite the release of over $38 million in federal home heating assistance for Maine households.

Collins initially ran against former Democratic Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race after a woman accused him of rape.

Republican Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall is trailing Democratic Kansas Senate nominee Adam Hamilton by an average of 2.6 points. A Democratic victory would be a major upset, given that Kansas has not had a Democratic senator since 1939.

The Republican senator sued 700 of his patients for outstanding debts during his time as an OB-GYN, which led to 81 arrests, The New York Times reported. Some facing lawsuits were mothers with outstanding bills from their deliveries, and many patients lacked insurance. One mother had a nine-month-old baby when her bank account was garnished.

Marshall paid a bakery $1,300 after its owner, Holly Thomas, accused his 2020 campaign of leaving a nearly $700 bill unpaid for six years. The senator said on X that he paid the bill and apologized to the bakery, claiming he had “no idea” how the bill went unpaid for six years.

RealClearPolling averages showed Marshall and Hamilton in a tie in mid-October.

The close race caused the Senate Leadership Fund, Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, to spend $14 million to support Marshall.

The Senate Majority PAC, the Democrats’ Senate campaign arm, launched a $5 million statewide television advertising campaign that plans to run through Election Day, indicating that Democrats were increasingly confident they could flip the seat, Politico reported. One ad attacked Marshall for voting against an amendment that would require the Department of Justice (DOJ) to release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The PAC’s research found that Epstein ads can sway elections three to six points in the Democrats’ direction.

The economy remained a top issue for Kansas voters, according to an Emerson College poll from Thursday. Diesel prices averaged $6.03 per gallon in Kansas, which Marshall largely attributed to the war in Ukraine. Hamilton pinned the high Diesel prices on Trump and the Iran war, which has likely resonated with farmers across the state.

Elections forecasters projected that Democrats would retake the House in the next Congress. Republicans redrew several districts to give themselves an advantage in November, but many Republican-held seats are still at risk of flipping for Democrats.

Republicans hoped to flip Democratic Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz’s seat in Florida’s 25th district. The state redrew the district with hopes that a Republican could pick up the seat, although Cook Political Report moved the race from the “Toss Up” column to “Lean Democratic.”

The Congressional Leadership Fund, the top House super PAC, slashed $6 million in ad spending in the district to oppose Moskowitz, who is running against former Republican Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer. The No Going Back PAC, a super PAC backed by MAGA Inc., planned to spend $6.3 million in the district.

The super PAC also slashed $3 million from Texas’ 28th district, which was redrawn to help Republicans oust Democratic Texas Rep. Henry Cuellar. Trump won the district by seven percentage points in 2024.

Cook Political Report shifted the races in Arizona’s sixth district, Colorado’s eighth district, Virginia’s second district and Wisconsin’s third district into the “Lean Democratic” column less than two weeks before Election Day. Republican Reps. Juan Ciscomani of Arizona, Gabe Evans of Colorado, Jen Kiggans of Virginia and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin currently hold those seats.

Eight Republican-held seats shifted in Democrats’ favor, including Republican Pennsylvania Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick’s seat in Pennsylvania’s first district and Republican Indiana Rep. Victoria Spartz’s seat in Indiana’s fifth district, according to Cook Political Report. The projection would give Democrats up to 240 seats in the House in the next Congress if they flip between 12 and 25 seats.

Republican Ohio Rep. Max Miller could lose to Democratic Ohio congressional nominee Brian Poindexter in Ohio’s 7th district, where Trump won by 10.6 percentage points in 2024. Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, accused him of domestic abuse, which Miller repeatedly denied.

Miller refused to drop out of the race when some in his party called on him to drop out. Among those who called on him to drop out included Husted and Miller’s ex-father-in-law, Republican Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno. Miller did not exit the race by the necessary deadline for Ohio’s Republican party to replace him, meaning Poindexter would have remained uncontested if Miller had exited the race.

Poindexter out-raised Miller by a wide margin in the third quarter. The Democrat reported $2.47 million in receipts and $1.72 million in spending between July 1 and September 30, while Miller raised $1.14 million and ended September with about $944,000 on hand.

Republican New York Rep. Mike Lawler faces a competitive reelection bid against Democratic New York congressional nominee Cait Conley in New York’s 17th district. He is one of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents since Harris won his district in the 2024 election by less than one point, although former President Joe Biden won it by ten points in 2020.

The candidates were neck-and-neck as of Friday. A McLaughlin & Associates survey from late September showed Lawler leading by three points, while an Emerson College poll showed Conley leading by two points.

Lawler painted Conley as a radical socialist on the campaign trail, while Conley tied Lawler to Trump. The district is one of the most centrist in the U.S.

Democratic New York Rep. Tom Suozzi is defending his seat in New York’s third district against former Republican New York state Assemblyman Michael LiPetri. Suozzi, who replaced former Republican New York Rep. George Santos after he was expelled from Congress, narrowly won his seat in 2024 by a three-point margin. The No Going Back PAC, a super PAC tied to Trump’s political organization MAGA Inc., spent nearly $8 million to support LiPetri, which included $5.7 million in ad spending to attack Suozzi.

Republican New York congressional nominee Anthony Constantino and Democratic New York congressional nominee Blake Gendebien are running for an open seat in New York’s 21st district after Republican New York Rep. Elise Stefanik decided not to run. While traditionally a Republican district, the candidates are neck-and-neck while tariffs, the economy and relations with Canada remained top issues.

A Public Policy Polling survey from mid-October found Constantino leading by two points, while a New York Times/Siena College poll showed Gendebien leading by four points.

Republican Pennsylvania Rep. Rob Bresnahan is defending his seat against Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti in Pennsylvania’s 8th district. The cost of living remained the top issue in the district, prompting Bresnahan to call on the Iran war to come to an immediate end. About two-thirds of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, which is expected to cost many Republicans House seats.

An Emerson College poll showed Cognetti leading 52% to 48%, while A New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University poll found her ahead by a 51% to 46% margin.

Republican Michigan Rep. Tom Barrett is facing off with Democratic Michigan congressional nominee William Lawrence, a further-left political activist, in Michigan’s seventh district. Lawrence co-founded the Sunrise Movement, an organization that advocates for action on climate change.

Recent polls showed Lawrence leading Barrett, including an Emerson College poll where Lawrence led by eight points.

news.originalContent:
Two Democrat candidates who vied to be the party’s nominee for Michigan’s open Senate seat appear to be sinking their coalition just days ahead of the election after sparring over Israel.

Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign asked Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens to avoid all campaign events ahead of the race, POLITICO, citing people familiar with the decision, reported Friday. The report comes after the former primary rivals exchanged jabs over an ad by Rebellion PAC, a left-wing political action committee created by The Young Turks’s founder Cenk Uygur, in which a woman claimed she couldn’t buy eggs because she had to set aside tax money for “killing Palestinians.” (RELATED: Abdul El-Sayed Said Assimilating To America Is Health Hazard In Academic Papers)

“On the eve of the eve of the eve of our BIG and important election, a unifying moment has arrived, our democratic nominee for U.S Senate disavows the Rebellion PAC ad made by Hasan Piker’s uncle that claims Jews are responsible for America’s economic woes,” Stevens stated in a Friday morning X post after El-Sayed’s campaign denied it was not affiliated with the ad.

On the eve of the eve of the eve of our BIG and important election, a unifying moment has arrived, our democratic nominee for U.S Senate disavows the Rebellion PAC ad made by Hasan Piker’s uncle that claims Jews are responsible for America’s economic woes. We have learned from party leaders and emissaries, as reported in the news media that he has. On Sunday I will join with the Great Democratic leader, Jim Clyburn and Dr El Sayed for a church service in the beautiful city of Detroit. The political coalition of Black and Jewish voices that have carried Michigan and this country through so many storms to the righteous path of liberal democracy and equal opportunity for all will ring out. Full statement here:

El-Sayed soon issued a statement on X firing back at Stevens.

“Our campaign is and has always been focused on addressing the most critical challenges Michiganders are facing: Skyrocketing gas prices, unaffordable groceries, and the inability to see a doctor,” El-Sayed wrote Friday. “That focus is why our people-powered campaign defeated a historic $70M in outside spending from big corporations and AIPAC [the American Israel Public Affairs Committee] on behalf of Congresswoman Stevens.”

El-Sayed then claimed his focus is on beating Republican nominee Mike Rogers.

Stevens’s office, as well as the El-Sayed and Rogers campaigns, did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s requests for comment.

Rogers, meanwhile, called Stevens a “courageous leader” for her performance during the August primary in a Friday night X post.

“She was absolutely right to call on Abdul El-Sayed to denounce the Rebellion PAC ad and she was right to call on him to apologize for espousing the same hateful ideology behind it,” Rogers wrote.

Representative Haley Stevens is a courageous leader who deserves the respect of every Michigan voter. She has conducted herself with nothing but class since the Democratic primary, a primary where a majority of voters did not vote for her party’s nominee. She was absolutely right to call on Abdul El-Sayed to denounce the Rebellion PAC ad and she was right to call on him to apologize for espousing the same hateful ideology behind it. Representative Stevens’ statement expressed a hope that Abdul El-Sayed “had heard the deep concerns of the Jewish Community.” It is as shameful as it is disappointing that his response to her clearly shows that he does not care about those concerns. In her statement, the Congresswoman says, “ the Jewish and African-American communities of my district deserve to have someone show up for them, rather than fight over them.” I agree with her and my campaign is about being there, showing up and defending these communities and all Michiganders.

President Donald Trump likwise said during a Friday rally in Daytona, Florida, that “[i]f you’re black, or if you’re Jewish, and you vote for Abdul, you’re not smart.”

Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. shared a similar sentiment on X that morning, stating he was unconvinced by El-Sayed’s Oct. 1 disavowal of the Muslim Brotherhood.

“Under persistent badgering before national news cameras, Al-Sayed finally caved: ‘Sure. Yeah, absolutely!’ he said unconvincingly. He then spent five minutes attacking the man’s motives,” Kennedy wrote in his roughly 3,000-word post. “El-Sayed said nothing about the Brotherhood itself, its ideology, or the Muslim Brotherhood front organizations he works with. A disavowal that names nothing and condemns nothing is a disavowal in name only.”

El-Sayed leads Rogers by 5% as of Saturday, according to FiftyPlusOne’s polling average.

news.originalContent:

Savannah Chrisley and her husband, Jason Galanis, are having a baby boy.

The “Chrisley Knows Best” star announced she will be a boy mom in an Instagram reel posted Monday.

The reel presented cutting a cake with blue frosting inside, the couple happily kissing, and Chrisley’s parents, Todd and Julie, beaming and showing blue baby clothing and baby toys to the camera.

“My sweet miracle boy… you are everything we prayed for and more. The most beautiful reminder that God’s plans are always greater than our own,” Savannah captioned the video.

“The past few days have reminded me just how cruel this world can be. But no amount of hate could ever overshadow the joy of loving you. You are a MIRACLE.”

“My precious baby boy, your daddy and I will spend the rest of our lives protecting you, praying over you, and loving you beyond measure. We may not be able to shield you from every bit of darkness in this world, but we promise to raise you to be a LIGHT in it,” she continued.

“You are already our greatest blessing, our answered prayer, and the sweetest chapter of our lives. God knew exactly what He was doing when He gave us YOU. WE GET TO BE YOUR MOMMY AND DADDY!!!” she concluded.

The news comes after Chrisley, 29, revealed on Oct. 27 that she is engaged and expecting their first child,  It was subsequently revealed that her fiancé is convicted fraudster Galanis, 56, and that she and Galanis secretly tied the knot on July 14 at a Baptist church in the Cayman Islands, months before publicly announcing their engagement and pregnancy.

Taking to Instagram with an intimate video of her and Galanis celebrating their upcoming arrival, the 29-year-old said, “I’ve prayed for this life. I’ve cried for this life. And there were moments I truly wondered if this life would ever be mine. 🥹🤍.

“The past few years have taken me through fires I never imagined I’d have to walk through. Seasons of heartbreak, loss, and moments when I didn’t know if I would ever make it to the other side. I wondered if I would ever find my forever… if I would ever feel safe enough to truly breathe again,” Chrisley continued in the caption.

She said God sent her Galanis n the middle of “heartbreak” and that he helped her “heal.”

Chrisley called her husband her “protector” and “fiercest fighter,” as well as her “most loyal person.”

“My safe place. A man with the patience of Job (and Lord knows he needs it 🤣). The one who makes me laugh even on my hardest days,” the Good Girl Rx owner continued.

“For the first time in a long time, I feel safe. I feel fulfilled. I can finally exhale. I found my forever in you,” she wrote, along with an emoji of an engagement ring.

She then praised how supportive Galanis has been throughout her pregnancy so far, sharing that he has been to every doctor’s appointment and constantly gushes over her “beautiful” bump.

“I once prayed just to make it through another day. Now I get to spend forever with the love of my life, carrying a little miracle we already love more than words,” she wrote.

“From heartbreak to healing. From surviving to living. From praying for my forever to building a family with him,” Chrisley added.

In an accompanying episode of her “Unlocked” podcast, she shared more details about her new relationship, explaining that she met Galanis in the “world of politics” while she was campaigning for President Donald Trump to pardon her formerly imprisoned parents, Todd and Julie Chrisley.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

For three quarters, the Knicks were playing down to their opponent. They were, in a word, terrible. Knicks-Nets was so ugly it should’ve been blurred out for indecency.

But then the defending champs woke up. OG Anunoby caught fire, Josh Hart provided a spark and the Knicks ultimately cakewalked to a 103-90 victory Monday at MSG.

With Jalen Brunson on the bench at the start of the final period, the Knicks (3-4) went from a four-point deficit to a 10-point advantage in about four minutes. It spurred the Knicks’ 15th straight victory over the Nets (1-6), a streak that began in 2023 — right after the Durant-Kyrie era in Brooklyn.

But Monday was in doubt for the majority of the night.

The first half was a slopfest from both sides. The Knicks shot 36 percent but still held a seven-point advantage at the break because of their abundance of free throws.

Brunson and Landry Shamet were the lone bright spots. The Nets were a misfiring mess but found a rhythm after the break — particularly Michael Porter Jr. — and won the third quarter 35-24.

Mike Brown responded with a new lineup — with Tyler Kolek and Jordan Clarkson in the backcourt — and the Nets folded with just 11 total points in the fourth quarter.

Anunoby scored eight of his 18 points in the first six minutes of the fourth. Karl-Anthony Towns finished with 16 rebounds and 11 points. Brunson had 19 points, but was again inefficient on 6-for-16 shooting. Shamet scored all 20 of his points in the first three quarters. Mikal Bridges pulled another Houdini and was benched for all but three minutes of the second half. He had six points on 1-for-7 shooting from the field.

For the Nets, Julius Randle, the former Knicks All-Star, forced the issue and often missed — shooting 5-for-16 with a team-high 21 points.

The interborough matchup, once touted as a powerful rivalry when the Nets moved from Jersey to Brooklyn, now carries the juice of a steamrolled grape. The Knicks have always dominated the attention of New York City, and it’s never been more lopsided than in 2026 — the year of James Dolan’s first title.

The Nets have become an afterthought under the stewardship of GM Sean Marks, who is second to only Brian Cashman as the longest-tenured top sports executive in town. They haven’t won a playoff game since 2021, and there’s little hope Marks’ latest incarnation will break the streak.

They have two win-now veterans in Randle and Michael Porter Jr., who are surrounded by the young and unproven, operating a great distance from contending basketball.

Still, the Knicks were in trouble and playing ugly ball until the fourth-quarter whistle.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Jon Ledecky marvels that Matthew Schaefer is a better person than he is a hockey player, which the Islanders’ co-owner acknowledges is “saying an awful lot” about the reigning NHL Calder Trophy winner.

The second-year defenseman spent his off day Monday with family members at the R.J. Zuckerberg Cancer Center at the Northwell Health Center for Advanced Medicine in Lake Success to dedicate the Jennifer Schaefer Child Support Room in honor of his mother, who died of breast cancer in 2024.

The hockey-themed room will provide comfort, support and moments of joy for children while their parent or caregiver undergoes cancer treatment.

“I know my mom is smiling down today,” the 19-year-old Schaefer said. “This mean so much to my dad [Todd], my brother [Johnny] and especially to my mom.

“This room is going to be so special. It’s going to help so many families and so many kids. I know when my mom was going through cancer, we wished we could have had a room where me, my brother and my dad could go to get a breath of fresh air. I think I’m going to be there just as much as [these families] are.”

Schaeffer played a game of bubble hockey — and lost — earlier Monday in the support room with 15-year-old L.J. London, whose mother Tenika Isaacs, a teacher, recently rang the bell for completing her chemotherapy and radiation treatments for breast cancer, which is now in remission.

“As a parent, an educator and someone who has now faced breast cancer, I know firsthand that when a parent receives a diagnosis, the entire family feels its impact,” Isaacs said. “That is why the Jennifer Schaefer Child Support Center is so important.

“This space represents more than child care. It represents emotional support, compassion, connection and recognition that our children need care and reassurance throughout this journey, too.”

Schaefer also presented L.J. with a ladybug bracelet in honor of their mothers. Soon after his mother died, a ladybug landed on Schaefer’s leg, and he uses it as a symbol that she is always with him.

“It’s not fun when you come to hospitals,” Schaefer said. “But to have a room like this, where kids and families can go when your family [member] is getting treatment, the kids can go and just be a kid playing video games or just get a breath of fresh air and be themselves in a fun space that doesn’t feel like you’re at the hospital.”

Former Islanders forward Matt Martin and his wife Sydney — whose family the teenaged Schaefer lives with during the season — also were in attendance.

“Just to see how he’s handled everything he’s gone through on a day-to-day basis, he chooses to use this as a platform to help other people,” Martin said. “I know this has been something he’s been looking forward to since it was first talked about last year.

“It really is remarkable to see who he is as a person, not just as a hockey player, and that’s a testament to his mom and the way he was raised by [his family.”

The Islanders’ Children’s Foundation also made a donation of $150,000 to fund the project.

“My wife would be so pleased,” Schaefer’s father Todd said, fighting back tears. “That room is exactly what she would want, and I know when she was battling, we didn’t have anything like this. So to have a space like this where people can come in and kids can be kids, and it doesn’t matter how old they are, to be in her name, it couldn’t have come in a better place. … It’s a beautiful space to allow kids going through this to open up and talk about it… and to just get to be kids. … I know my wife is smiling and couldn’t be prouder.”

The Isles, who next face the Hurricanes on Thursday at UBS Arena, signed defenseman Ben Hutton to a PTO contract.

news.originalContent:

Securing genuine depth at running back becomes the ultimate separator between fantasy football contenders and pretenders. With more than half the schedule behind us, injuries mounting and bye weeks hitting hard, second-half touches at the position carry an extremely premium-value.

But as managers flock to the waiver wire, making smart additions requires critical context. You cannot afford to just go boxscore surfing and grab every player who popped off for a big stat line. You must ensure the player you acquire projects to hold a genuine, sustainable role moving forward.

Take Emmett Johnson as the prime example. Johnson is slated to be one of the most popular fantasy waiver additions this week. That’s largely because his 73-yard catch-and-run touchdown exploded onto screens during the late window when just three games were on, putting him directly under the spotlight of casual managers everywhere.

Though Andy Reid might continue to work the rookie into the Chiefs’ passing attack, the underlying usage paints a vastly different picture. Johnson still plays no more than 25 percent of offensive snaps, and this offense unambiguously belongs to Kenneth Walker III as both a runner and a receiver.

That minimal workload makes predicting when Johnson will actually produce almost impossible. His true fantasy value remains what it was before the big play: a top-tier handcuff to Walker rather than an immediate starter.

If you are looking for a pickup with a real path to a starting workload, Seth McGowan is the far more sensible target. The Jonathan Taylor trade rumors have turned from faint whispers into loud declarations as the deadline approaches. Once Taylor is moved, McGowan, who has already established himself as the primary backup, is slated to step right into the lead running back duties for the Colts.

Indianapolis did suffer a blow along the offensive line with the trade of star guard Quenton Nelson, but fantasy managers know that raw volume can frequently trump suspect line play. Better yet, McGowan’s audition as a starter could begin in Week 9 against a struggling Cowboys defense. Dallas is giving up a league-high 152.8 rushing yards per game and a porous 5.0 yards per carry average, while already allowing 10 rushing touchdowns on the ground.

At this juncture in the fantasy calendar, pure volume is the single most important metric to chase at running back. When evaluating potential pickups, look beyond single-game highlights and target players who project to earn heavy snap counts and an even stronger carry share. And don’t hesitate to pull the trigger even if you feel comfortable with your current starters. Given the relentless wave of injuries and backfield shifts defining the season, you can never have too much depth at the running back position.
